extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and writers interested in literary character types (antiheroes)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for understanding, analyzing, or creating antihero (and antiheroine) characters in fiction, including historical forms, typical traits, and notable examples. Useful for literary study or creative-writing decisions about morally ambiguous protagonists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: opposition to the traditional hero
rubrics_metrics.description: Antihero is a literary term that can be understood as standing in opposition to the traditional hero, i.e., one with high social status, well-liked by the general populace, and given a particular role to play. Although antiheroes may sometimes perform actions that most of the audience considers heroic, they continue because they must, not because they believe they are the right person for the job.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this definition to distinguish antiheroes from classic heroes: an antihero may act heroically but is not motivated by a sense of being 'the right person' or by duty; examples include the 'Man with No Name' archetype in Spaghetti Westerns. Consider social status, public likability, and role expectations when contrasting with a traditional hero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Racinian antihero — three defining factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Racinian' antihero is defined by three factors: (1) the antihero is doomed to fail before their adventure begins; (2) the antihero blames that failure on everyone but themselves; (3) they offer a critique of social morals and reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a specific archetype useful for constructing tragic/ironic protagonists: ensure the narrative sets up inevitable failure, a tendency to externalize blame, and a voice or function that critiques social norms. Use these factors when aiming for a classical/Racine-style antiheroic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral ambiguity / perspective-dependent status
rubrics_metrics.description: To other scholars, an antihero is inherently a hero from a specific point of view, and a villain from another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design antiheroes so that moral judgement depends on viewpoint—readers or other characters may interpret them as heroic or villainous. Leverage unreliable narration or contrasting perspectives to foreground this ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focal point of conflict in the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically, an antihero is the focal point of conflict in a story, whether as the protagonist or as the antagonistic force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using an antihero, make them central to the plot's conflict: their choices and engagement (typically of their own will) should drive the narrative, whether they serve as protagonist or antagonist. Highlight their agency in causing or escalating conflict even if their goals are self-centered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation: personal motives prioritized over the greater good
rubrics_metrics.description: The antihero focuses on their personal motives first and foremost, with everything else secondary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterize antiheroes by internal, self-centered goals rather than altruistic aims. Their decisions should primarily serve personal needs, desires, or survival, which can create tension with broader social or moral expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existentialist antihero traits (boredom, angst, alienation, indecisiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: In early 20th-century existentialist works the protagonist is an indecisive central character who drifts through his life and is marked by boredom, angst, and alienation (examples: Kafka's The Metamorphosis, Sartre's Nausea, Camus's The Stranger).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evoke an existentialist antihero, emphasize passivity or indecision, inner torment, alienation from society, and a sense of drift. Use interiority and mood (boredom/angst) rather than overt action to convey their antiheroic nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency/proactivity variation (historical/cultural differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: The American antihero of the 1950s and 1960s was typically more proactive than his French counterpart; the British antihero has other distinct traditions (e.g., 'angry young men').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider cultural and historical context when shaping an antihero's level of agency: U.S. mid-century antiheroes tend to act more, French/continental ones may be more passive or introspective. Use this axis to select tone and plot-driving behavior appropriate to the work's setting and influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antihero as social criticism / foil to traditional hero
rubrics_metrics.description: The antihero became an established form of social criticism, serving as a foil to the traditional hero archetype and reflecting shifts in heroic ethos (e.g., from feudal aristocrat to urban democrat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use antiheroes to critique social values, institutions, or the notion of heroism itself. Position them as counterpoints to conventional ideals, letting their flaws and marginality expose cultural contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antiheroine: gendered subversion of expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: By the 2020s scholarship had expanded to include the 'antiheroine,' examining complex women protagonists who subvert traditional gender expectations of nurturing and compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating female antiheroes, foreground ways they resist stereotypical feminine roles (nurturing, compliance) and explore the gender politics of complexity, agency, and transgressive behavior. Refer to contemporary TV and scholarship on antiheroines for examples and nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to perform heroic actions for non-heroic reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Although antiheroes may sometimes perform actions that most of the audience considers heroic, they continue because they must, not because they believe they are the right person for the job.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate antiheroes from true heroes by clarifying motive: even when they act 'heroically', their internal justification should be pragmatic, coerced, self-interested, or fatalistic rather than noble duty. This preserves moral ambiguity.
